The Hawk’s Rebirth

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-10-31

The Hawk’s Rebirth

In the last week of Chaitra, on an afternoon of dry spring heat, a shadow wheels over the beach at Char Kukri-Mukri. It looks like the shadow of a cloud that drifted on and forgot to take it along. It slides across blue, salted water, then slips over the wet gray sand beneath the casuarinas. The shadow belongs to an old hawk, riding the air in wide circles with his wings spread. Nothing in the way he floats is sharp or insolent anymore, those marks of his youth. The wind still carries him, but some old understanding between them has broken. A dull, stubborn ache sits at the joint of his wing, and on cold mornings it comes to report for duty. The feathers at his wing tips have worn rough, gray has crept up from his head, and the yellow talons slip now and then on the bark they once gripped. Once, those talons split the backs of fish. Now they can barely find purchase on a wet branch.

Below, out of deep water, a school of small silver fish flashes up like a handful of light, as though someone had thrown coins into the sea. Then it sinks back into the dark. The hawk folds his wings and drops, but the fish are gone to the depths before his shadow touches the surface. He climbs again, turns against the wind, dives a second time, and the result is the same. On the third climb, hauling himself up out of the air, he feels a wrench at the root of his wing so sharp that the world goes black for an instant. The sky seems to turn once around him. Somehow he steadies and lands on a thick branch of the old casuarina leaning out over the edge of the grove. The branch dips under his weight and rights itself. He sets his talons deep in the bark, as if the tree might let him go the moment his attention slips.

For three days nothing fresh has passed his beak. The skin of his breast has dried tight over the edge of the bone, and after any long flight his breath takes ages to find its rhythm. His eyes, though, still read the slightest disturbance in the water. He can see the fin of a small fish stir in mud far off. But the silent accord that once held between what the eye sees and what the wing can do has broken, no one knows when, without announcement. The failure has not only made him hungry. It has made him a stranger to himself. A stretch of sky that once cost a few wingbeats now feels like an expedition of its own.

Then, late in the afternoon, the wind swings from south to northwest. It brings the dry smell of dust, as if earth were being lifted somewhere far away. The hawk knows the smell. Before a Kalbaishakhi, the violent nor’wester of the dry season, the coastal wind turns exactly like this, quietly at first, then all at once taking the entire sky for its own. He tilts his head. The beach dissolves in that smell, and a storm from many years ago comes back inside his skull.

In those days he is in the full strength of his youth. When he stretches his wings they look like plates of black steel. His feathers are dense and oiled, and any wild wind off the coast is his most faithful friend. From above the clouds he reads the faintest eddy in the river mouth, then comes down in the blink of an eye and sinks his talons into the hard back of a bhetki or a mullet. He feels the fish thrash beneath his claws, and as he rises from the water the spray flung off its tail clings to the feathers of his chest. There is weariness in that flying, but no weakness. When he settles on a high branch after the hunt, it seems to him that all the wind of the sea is moving through his wings.

But he does not fly only for hunger, because his mate floats beside him, parallel in the air. When the two of them wheel across the sky, the outermost feathers of their wings sometimes brush, and the slight friction sends a fine current under the skin that softens even the dry salt wind of Falgun. Sometimes one drops a little to wait for the other. Sometimes, flying side by side, they bank in opposite directions without warning and then return to the same circle. No calling passes between them, yet who will turn where, who will lose altitude and when, seems to have been settled in advance.

After the hunt they sit side by side on a high, secluded branch in the forest, stripping scales from fish and tearing warm flesh. Sometimes one stops in the middle of eating and pushes the soft part of the fish toward the other’s beak. Then every knot of muscle grows heavy with easy idleness. They cross the mouth of the Meghna to the open sea, circle without effort above the masts of trawlers, and return to their casuarina before dark. Their nest sits high in its branches. It is not large, but year upon year of twigs, dry grass and fibers of leaf have settled into it until it has a smell of its own. On rainy nights they curl up together. When the sound of the wind changes before a storm, one looks at the other, and then shifts a little in the nest to make room.

Nothing in their blood yet knows that anything can be lost. Once, in the dying light of an afternoon, his mate brings a thin dry twig in her beak and sets it at the rim of the nest, beside last year’s sticks. Whether there is any particular reason for it, the hawk does not know. Perhaps she saw it in passing. Perhaps she noticed a gap in the broken part of the nest and meant to fill it. He is sitting beside her, preening. He glances up once, then goes back to his feathers. Still the twig stays at the rim of the nest. It carries no words. It is only a quiet, settled consent that many more winters will be spent here, that many more monsoon rains will pass over their heads.

Then comes that afternoon in Kartik. The whirl of a cyclone, rushing in from the west, tears the two of them apart in midair and flings them in different directions. The first blow is fierce, but they can ride it out. Both stiffen their wings and fight to hold their balance. Then the wind turns so suddenly that every familiar calculation of the sky is overturned in an instant. Rain and salt mist close over everything. The hawk beats his wings with all he has, trying to turn back toward his mate, but the pull of the low pressure shoves him blindly toward a broken canal. Once he gathers every ounce of strength and tries to climb, and the wind drives him down again. Rain fills his eyes and blurs his sight. Through that thick gray he sees, far off, a wing scrawling helplessly across the sky. Before he can know whether it is hers, the curtain of cloud swallows it.

When the storm is over he still cannot find her. For weeks afterward he roams every thicket of Char Kukri-Mukri, the tangled roots of the mangroves, the small shoals in the estuary. He tests the wind, scans branch after branch, drops to the sand to look for the trace of a wet feather. Not a single dropped feather turns up anywhere. When he sees another hawk flying in the distance he follows it, and after a while understands that it is not her, and comes back alone. In the world of birds, news of a lost mate’s death does not arrive. When a body vanishes along the roads of the wind, its history is left in the keeping of the sky’s silence. Whether she found shelter in the forest of some distant island or drowned at sea that stormy night, the hawk never learns.

After the storm he flies alone. He has stopped counting the winters, the monsoons, the Chaitras that have gone by. The vastness of the sky is no longer freedom to him. It has become one enormous empty house. Even now, when he flies, he keeps the outermost feathers of his wings slightly bent, as if someone drifting beside him might brush against them. Only the wind passes through that empty space.

Toward evening the wind settles again and the Kalbaishakhi does not come. The hawk opens his eyes and sees the sea lying gray in the dull light, exactly as before. The memory of the old storm slowly withdraws, but the emptiness it left goes nowhere. He leaves the branch, rises, dives again, but in the muddy water of low tide the small catfish and barbs vanish into the mire at the sight of his heavy shadow. Once he knew the wind of this estuary as his own. From which direction the shoals would rise, where the current turned, over which wave to come down so the catch would be easy, he knows it all. But water has no respect for an old hunter. Every time he drops, the fish dissolve into the mud.

Hunger burns in his belly, and that burning forces him to turn his wings away from the coast, toward the settled land inland. Heading north, he comes first over empty fields where the winter crops have been cut and the soil lies cracked by the drought of Chaitra. Here a haystack, there a bamboo platform, there a flock of ducks at the edge of a pond choked with water hyacinth. In the distance some cows stand with their heads lowered to the dry grass. Smoke from cooking fires rises out of the villages, and the shrieks of children carry from a yard. All these years such sounds have belonged to a faraway world. Today hunger drags him close to it.

The yard of a newly built house lies empty. Finding no movement of life there, he shifts a little farther east, to the older part of the village. A prosperous farmer’s house with a tin roof, a raised plinth, a yard smoothed with fresh clay, a granary of rice in one corner. In the dust of the yard a country hen scratches for food with half a dozen yellowish chicks. The chicks dart to their mother’s feet, then push their beaks into cracks in the dry ground, hunting insects. When the hen rakes the earth they all crowd in, then scatter again in an instant. As a strange shadow crosses the sky, the hen puffs out her throat and clucks sharply, lowering her wings to call them in. Most of the chicks run to the warm dark of feathers beneath her belly. Only one, a straggler, goes on hunting insects at the foot of a dry gourd vine.

The hawk drops soundlessly through a gap in the leaves. The act feels close to a betrayal of the hunter born in him. To leave the open fight with silver fish in the sea and raid this small circle of tame life is, beyond the pressure of hunger, a kind of shamed surrender of his own dignity. Still, hunger knows nothing of dignity. It plants the body in a place where there is no room to choose. His talons close on the chick’s soft back. The small body is warm, and inside it a heart is racing. He feels it under his claws. The hen shrieks. She lowers her wings and takes a few steps toward him, neck rigid, eyes on the sky. Her cry runs across the yard, and it holds more than warning. It holds a desperate claim: give back the life I have been sheltering under my wings.

The hawk’s talons loosen.

The chick tips over into the dust, lies still for a few moments, then moves a leg. It staggers upright, flaps its small wings in confusion, loses its direction once, then follows its mother’s call and runs into the feathers. The hen lowers her wings and covers it. The hawk is still on the ground. He looks on for a few moments, then spreads his wings and settles on a branch of the old jamun tree at the edge of the yard. He does not come down again. Below, the hen counts her chicks one by one. They have scattered again, some at her feet, some beside the granary, and again and again she draws them in, then lifts her head to the sky. In the hawk’s belly the hunger burns on as before. He has made no kill, and yet his strength is spent. But a strange stillness descends on him, as though a door shut for many years has opened for a moment and quietly closed again.

When the sun leans toward the bend of the western river, the hawk spreads his wings and drops south. He leaves behind the reed beds at the edge of the marsh, the fallow land, the earth split by the sun, and flies on. After a while the familiar smell of salt and fish returns to the wind. It draws him back toward the sea. But he cannot quite believe that a familiar smell means a familiar shelter.

Before dusk he returns to the branch of their old casuarina, fluffs his feathers, and rounds himself into a ball. It is a night of Chaitra and the air is warm, yet the wind off the sea slips through the branches and shakes him to the bones of his chest, because his body no longer has its coat of fat. On many winter nights his mate would sit pressed against him on this very branch, and the warmth of two bodies would beat the cold. The memory comes suddenly and lodges in his ribs like a bodily pain. He tucks his head under his wing, but sleep does not come. In the kewra thicket below, a pair of jackals start up barking. His talons tighten on the branch, his eyes settle on the murky dark. After a while the barking stops, and the sound of the waves goes on in the same rhythm far off. Then a bottomless weariness covers him. Late in the night the sea wind stalls. He shifts his weight from his right foot to his left, then back again. Before dawn the sky is shut under an opaque gray-black sheet, and in the damp sea air the bark of the tree turns slick.

At the first light in the east the hawk spreads his wings to stretch. At that exact moment his numb talons slip on the wet bark. Once he catches himself. The second time he cannot. Like a stone, he drops from the branch and strikes the sand. The old habit of beating his wings fires, but the fall is so short that the air has no time to fill them. He rolls a little down the wet slope of the beach and stops beside a broken conch shell. Lifting his head, he sees the surf break a few inches from his talons and withdraw, leaving white foam. On its way back the wave leaves a large hilsa on the shore, out of season, dead. It might have been thrown away from some fisherman’s net. The belly has begun to rot, yet in the morning light the scales still shine.

He tries to move. His wings do not answer. He tries again, but his body seems stuck to the sand. Another wave comes and leaves its foam at his feet. The fish lies a little way off. Pressing on his belly, he begins to drag himself through the sand. He advances, stops, advances again. The tips of his talons sink into the grit, and wet sand clots on the feathers of his chest. After a few inches his breath goes heavy, but he does not stop. Reaching the fish, he touches its cold, slippery skin with his blunt beak. No pulse. Gathering the last of his strength, he tears off a piece of the rotten, salty flesh. The first mouthful is hard to swallow and catches in his throat. He stops, lifts his head a little, breathes, then eats again. There is no pleasure in the taste. There is only a warmth that reaches deep into the body. After a few mouthfuls he stops, and some time later lowers his beak again. No miraculous strength returns with this food, but the fire in his stomach slowly burns down.

Then he sits beside the fish with his wet wings open, taking the morning sun. Warmth rising from the sand sinks deep into his feathers. When the sun has climbed a little, he tries to stand. The first time he reels and goes over on his side. The second time he plants his feet hard in the sand and stays up. His body is still trembling and there is pain at the root of his wings, but this time he does not fall. A heavy gust comes off the sea, steady, weighty and familiar, and his wings recognize its touch. He pushes with his legs. On the first leap his body does not rise. On the second it floats a little. On the third the wind gets under his wings and lifts him a few finger-widths above the sand. Skimming the tops of the casuarinas, flying very low, he goes a short way and comes down gasping. The pain in his shoulder is still there, the grip of his feet is slack, but his nerves have not forgotten the hidden roads of the wind.

For the next two days he does not leave that stretch of shore. When the hilsa is finished, he picks over crabs left stranded in the mud at low tide, and dead shrimp. He eats a little at a time whenever he finds food, then rests a long while, because after so long a fast his body cannot take much at once. By day he dries his wings, works the sand out from between his feathers with his beak, and sits through the noon sun with his eyes half shut. Now and then, in the distance, a kingfisher plunges into the water. Once such a sight woke the urge to hunt in him. Now he only watches. That this coast can no longer feed him does not become clear in any single moment. One day, sitting on a branch, he notices that his head is turned east, across the river mouth, toward the islands and, beyond them, a thin blue line. He has never seen that line from close by, only caught it from the corner of his eye on clear mornings after storms. The next day he is looking the same way. On the third day the wind brings him the damp smell of earth from some distant land. And then, at first light in Boishakh, the month that opens the Bengali year, he goes back to their old nest.

The dry twigs are still knotted into one another, worn smooth by many storms. Once, when dusk fell, two bodies pressed together here. Now half the nest lies empty. The hawk stares for a long while without blinking. A few old feathers are caught in the rim of the nest, their color washed out by rain. In the wind they stir a little, but they do not blow away. One day a Kalbaishakhi and salt rain will strip these twigs apart. Maybe some young bird will come and gather new straw. Maybe the branch will break and the nest will end up on the ground. None of it holds him back now. In one corner of the nest the twig is still there, the one his mate once brought in her beak. It has blended into the old sticks so thoroughly that no one could tell it apart by color or by grain. The hawk touches it once with the tip of his beak. The twig does not move. After a while he turns his face away, spreads his wings, and flies east over the estuary. Behind him the nest shrinks in the branches of the casuarina, then is lost in green.

On the first day of his journey he flies very low over the water, where the layer of air rising off the sea gives his wings a little to lean on. In the muddy water of the estuary, currents turn in whorls. Here and there fishing boats float below, and far off the green line of the mangroves of Hatiya shows. The men sitting on the roofs of the boats look up at his shadow, but he does not look at them. Twice along the way he comes down on small, newly risen shoals to loosen his wings. Several times a sharp pull seizes the root of his wing, and he drops lower, closer to the water, the tips of his wings almost touching the waves. When the far shore finally grows large, his body is no longer fighting to fly. It is fighting only not to fall. He lands on a branch of a keora tree and sits a long time with his wings folded and his eyes half shut. The smell of leaves, the smell of mud, and the smoke of some distant village come drifting in together on the air.

In the afternoon, at the edge of a secluded village on Hatiya, he goes hunting again. Here too there is a yard, a hen, a few chicks. Rice straw lies on one side of the yard, a heap of dried dung on the other. The chicks are pecking at the ground. The moment the hawk drops, the chicks bolt, and the hen lowers her wings and begins to call. One chick loses its way and stands at the edge of the yard. The hawk takes it in his talons. This time he does not stop anywhere. He flies to a bamboo grove far off and sits down to eat. Behind him the hen’s shrill cry rises. He bends his beak, tears flesh, swallows, tears again. The small bones snap under his beak. He eats down to the last scrap, then wipes his beak on the branch. In the earlier yard he let the chick go, and his body grew weaker for it. This time he leaves nothing. What he carries away is no wisdom, only a full belly.

The next day he leaves Hatiya and heads for Sandwip. At first the morning wind is kind. The island’s shoreline shows from far off like a green stroke. The hawk climbs slowly, as if to prepare his body before the crossing of open water. But just before the shore comes into focus, the sky in the west goes black along its lower edge. A smell rises in the wind that the roots of his feathers recognize before he does. He tilts his wings to change course, but the first blow lands before he can. The Kalbaishakhi arrives with a wall of dust and a cold gust. The first blast hits him from the side so hard that he almost rolls over and touches the waves. He folds his wings, makes his body small, and gives himself up to the wind. The storm lifts him, drops him, then with one shove flings him far away. In the end it deposits him on a newly risen mudflat some distance from Sandwip.

The rain comes down like a solid sheet. The hawk sits in the mud with his feathers puffed out and his head tucked in. After a while, when the force of the storm eases, he lifts his head. There is not a tree anywhere, no high ground, only gray, smooth mud that takes his feet down. He tries to beat his wings and rise, but his soaked feathers are heavy and his talons stick in the mud. Once his body lifts a little and falls again. The second time his feet slip before he can open his wings. The third time he understands that this mud will not easily let him go. Meanwhile the tide has begun to come in. First water gathers in the low places far off, then small waves creep across the mud. Water at one end of the shoal, water at the other. Again and again he beats his heavy wings to rise, and again and again he falls into the mud. The water begins to wash away the ground beneath his talons.

At last he sees a bamboo pole, left behind by fishermen, half buried in the mud. He grips it with his feet, steadies his wings, and somehow hauls his body up to its tip. The pole sways. With every gust of wind he comes close to losing his balance. Water on every side, waves below, the tide still rising. After a time the water touches his talons, then covers the lower part of the pole. All night he stands on that thin bamboo. Salt spray hits his feathers, and the last drops of rain have settled cold in the folds of his wings. Once he closes his eyes, but he cannot sleep, because the slightest nod would slide him off the pole into the water. He tightens his grip. Once, a faint light shows between the clouds and fades again. Late in the night the ebb begins. The water slowly draws back, and by morning the shoal has surfaced again, wet, shining, unrecognizable. The hawk climbs down from the pole and stands in the mud. His legs shake, his wings are heavy, but he is alive.

On a rain tree at the shore of Sandwip he spends nearly four weeks. For the first few days he only dries his feathers and scratches the salt off with his beak. He drinks a little at a time from the drops of rainwater clinging to the leaves. At low tide he finds small crabs stranded in the mud near the shore, and sometimes the remains of a dead fish. At first he is afraid to come down from the branch, because his legs cannot properly take his weight. He studies the ground below for a long time before he descends. When he finds food he does not go far, but climbs back up and rests. Slowly he begins to try his wings, first from one branch to the next, then to another tree a little farther off. After each landing a pull seizes the root of his wing and his breath runs fast in his chest. He waits until it settles. One morning the air is calm. He leaves the branch, flies a short way, and returns. The next day he goes a little farther. So the days go by.

One morning he stands facing the Sandwip channel. The green line on the far side shows from a distance, but between lie brown water, whirlpools and sudden gusts of cross-current. To cross it he will have to trust his own wings again. The hawk spends a long time measuring the wind. Which way the water runs, where the crests are rising, from which side the wind meets the underside of his wings, he studies it all. Then he jumps. Midway, a pull at the root of his wing is so fierce that his breath stops. He sheds altitude, sheds it again, until he is so close to the water that the tips of his wings take the slap of the waves. There is no way back now, because the shore behind is far and the one ahead is just as far. No branch, no sandbar, only water. He holds his wings still and glides low over the swells. Once his body heels over on one side and he recovers. Once the wind dies all at once and leaves a hollow beneath his wings. He is almost falling when an unexpected layer of air slides under him and lifts him a little. He does not hesitate. He straightens his body and flies for the shore ahead.

After he lands on the branch of a keora on the far side, his whole body is shaking. His beak hangs open, his tongue is dry, his eyes are half closed. For a while he sits gripping the branch. Down in the mud small crabs are walking about. Far off on the water a boat moves slowly on. The hawk does not look at it. All that matters to him now is to get his breath back, to stop the trembling, to save a little strength for the next flight.

Going from there toward Mirsarai, the signs of people thin out fast. First the rice fields and villages of the coast, then a few scattered houses, then dense jungle closes over all the land below. No smoke from any hearth, no tin roof, only green crowns and a rushing wind. Before the afternoon sun fades, the blue line of the hills sharpens in the northeast. To him it was once only a cloud far away. Now it grows slowly larger. On the hillsides he can make out here a cleft in the rock, there a treetop, there an open slope bright in the sun. The hawk knows that near human settlement every search for a meal means meeting danger. Yards, hens, men, traps, food and peril lie together in each. In the hills the sky is more open and men are fewer. Even if prey is scarcer there, at least he can find a shelter of his own. Before dusk he reaches the face of a steep rocky outcrop. As darkness thickens he lowers his body onto the top of a lonely hillock overgrown with scrub. Boishakh is running out.

Between two boulders of reddish-brown sandstone there is a deep cleft. Little wind enters it, and rain does not fall straight in. In his beak he gathers wild creepers, dry sticks and soft grass, and builds a lair there. The first night he cannot sleep. With his back against the rock he stares into the distant dark. No memory of joy or grief is tied to this place. No smell or sound pulls him back toward anything old. Wherever he has gone until now, some old trace has been there, a nest, a tree, the estuary, the familiar smell of the wind, and somewhere in all of it the absence of his mate has clung. Here there is not even a trace of that absence. The stone does not know him, the wind knows nothing of his past. As the night wears on a sliver of waning moon rises, the stream valley sinks into darkness, and far away the bright thread of the sea disappears. The hawk sits with his wings folded and his head bowed. In the stone walls only the slow sound of his own breathing comes back to him again and again.

The sun of Joishtho, the hottest month, sets the hillside on fire. At noon the rock grows so hot that he cannot leave the shade of the cleft. Over these few weeks the hawk slowly learns the hill. Which crack holds rainwater, which slope keeps the noon sun longest, behind which rock the north wind cannot reach him, from which branch the movements of the stream below can be seen, he learns it all in his own way. There is no abundance here like the sea. Some days he finds the egg of a wild bird in a hollow of a tree, some days a lizard in a crack in the rock, some days the scent of a hill mouse hiding in the grass. Sometimes he picks up a hard-shelled black beetle in his beak and eats it. On most days he finds nothing. At first he does not go far to hunt. His wings are still weak, and on an unfamiliar slope a small mistake could dash him against the rock. On the hungry days he does not beat his wings for nothing. He folds them in the shade of the rock and saves the heat of his body, and when the cold comes down at night he fluffs his feathers and rounds himself into a ball.

The days no longer separate in his memory. When morning comes he leaves his shelter, tests the smell of the wind, studies the far slopes. At noon he returns to the shade. In the evening, when the light changes on the hillside, he goes to sit on some high rock again. On clear days a bluish line shows to the southwest. The sea. Sometimes he watches it, sometimes he turns his face away. When he thinks of the old coast a tight pull catches at his chest, but he does not think of going back. He knows what he would find. The same nest, the same tree, the same empty half. The pain of a new place is at least new.

Late in Joishtho the first rain falls. Water runs down the dry rock in thin lines, and small pools collect in the cracks of the earth. The smell of the hill changes into wet soil, rotting leaves, a raw odor rising from deep inside the stone. After the rain small insects appear on the rock. The hawk hunts them out and eats them. Some days water stands in his cleft. He lowers his beak and drinks slowly. The weariness of his body has not left, but at the end of the day his breath settles a little more easily than before.

From that time his old feathers begin to fall. One morning, sitting on a rock, he spreads his wings and a faded gray feather drops from his shoulder of its own accord. It sways a little in the wind and catches in a crack of the stone. Where it was, a dark, delicate shoot has come up, threaded with blood vessels, the soft sheath of a new feather. The next day another old feather works loose. So, one after another, the feathers fall, but never all at once. His body seems to keep its own accounts. No feathers drop together in a way that would ruin the balance of the wing. The main feathers change slowly, week after week, and only when a new feather has grown out a little in one place does its neighbor come loose.

The season is not easy for him. The way his wings catch the air has changed. In places the feathers are thin, in places a new feather has not yet hardened. When he flies, his body sometimes leans too far to one side, and sometimes the wind will not pass properly through his wings. So he does not fly much. As each new feather pushes out through the skin, its base pulls and itches. Every day when the sun is up he sits on the rock and gently arranges his feathers with his beak, clearing dust and parasites. If a feather hurts too much, he lets it be and does not force it. On rainy days he fluffs his wet feathers and sits inside his lair. The monsoon of Ashar comes down on the hills, and week after week the sky stays gray.

Early in the rains, one day, bending over a pool of water in a hollow of rock to look at his own shadow, the hawk notices the old wound at the tip of his beak. Years of tearing hard prey have worn the point blunt. On one side there is a fine crack, with salt and grime packed inside. He tilts his head and studies his reflection on the water. The tip with which he once tore the hard scales of fish now looks ragged and uneven. He touches it lightly against the rough face of the rock. At once a violent pain makes him jerk his head and stop. For a while he sits quite still. Then he brings the tip toward the stone again, but this time he does not rub. The place seems to throb from within.

For the next few days he touches nothing hard. He gets through the days on soft insects, small lizards, any prey that tears easily. After the rain, tiny water creatures sometimes turn up in the pools in the rock. The grime packed in the wound on his beak slowly dries. Beneath the worn-away shell a new layer grows, bit by bit. One day, as he is shifting a twig, a thin, rough layer on the top of his beak comes away by itself. Beneath it appears a smoother part, a little paler in color. The tip is no longer as sharp as it was, and whether it ever will be again, the hawk does not know. But with the ordinary use of each day it is slowly becoming serviceable. He never again tries to sharpen his beak against stone.

The injury to his talons keeps him careful for some time too. The tip of one claw on his right foot broke long ago against rock, and at the base of his hind toe there is the deep scar of an old kill. When he perches, the hawk lets his weight settle on the good foot and keeps the wounded one tucked out of sight. Before gripping anything he tests the position of his claws. When he walks across rock he watches whether the broken tip will catch. The edge of the broken claw slowly smooths over, and from the base a new sheath grows. So slowly that, day after day, no one would notice. But one stormy evening in Srabon, when he grips the branch of a wet gurjan tree hard and sits for a long time facing the wind, it becomes clear that the full strength of the claw has not returned, but a grip that can hold has.

Late in Srabon, one morning, he notices her for the first time, the young hawk. On a grassy slope across the stream a young female sits alone, tearing a field mouse. There is a gleam of youth on her wings, and the morning light falling across her feathers makes a new kind of brightness. The old hawk makes no sound. He settles on a rock at a safe distance and shows no sign of coming closer. The female turns her head once, then goes back to eating, without fear or caution. His presence seems to her, in that moment, neither a danger nor an event.

Over the following weeks the hunting grounds of the two begin, without their knowing, to touch. Sometimes they sit at the two ends of the same ridge with twenty or thirty paces between them. Neither looks at the other. Sometimes the female drops to the slope below, and sometimes she lands on the branch of a tree near the old hawk’s lair. He does not give up his place, and she does not try to come near him. No calls pass between them. Only the same hill wind, the same sun, the same hunting ground has let the two of them live side by side.

One day the old hawk watches the female seize a gray dove in midair. The quickness of the strike is something he no longer has. He turns his head a little to look. He remembers his own youth, the swift flight, the unerring dive, drifting side by side with his mate. But this time the memory does not drag him down as it used to. The female flies off with her kill toward another slope. The old hawk watches a while, then goes back to combing his feathers. For the next three days she is not seen. He does not look for her.

In the middle of Bhadro, when more than half of his new feathers have come in, one day he is about to drop from a branch above the stream to hunt and does not drop. On a flat rock below, a lizard is basking. The distance is right, the angle is right, the wind is favorable. He watches the lizard. His body leans forward a little, muscle tightens, talons harden on the branch. Still the wings do not open. A strange numbness spreads inside him. In that moment he remembers how, the last time he dived like this, a wrench at the root of his wing sent darkness down over his eyes. He looks at his wings. The lizard turns its head on the stone, takes in its surroundings once, and slips into a crack. The hawk sits on that branch a long time. Then, slowly, he walks down the rock on foot, as though he had no wings, as though he could only go by his legs.

The next day he comes back to the same branch. The same distance, the same stone. The lizard is not the same one, but another small creature fit for hunting is moving below. He leans, spreads his wings slightly, stops again. On the third day it happens again. Some days he goes halfway into the dive and returns. Some days he drops an arm’s length from the branch and climbs back up. Each time the memory of the old pain holds his body back. Then one day a small snake shows in the grass. It is crawling slowly across a rock. The hawk is sitting on the branch with no particular readiness in him. Suddenly he opens his wings and drops. His talons close on the snake’s body and it coils and thrashes. He loses his balance for a moment but does not loosen his grip. Then he pins the head with his beak and stills the prey. For a long time he sits on the rock. His heart is knocking in his chest. The kill lies before him, and it is as if he is seeing his own recovered power for the first time. From then on the dive comes a little easier each time. Before every dive he pauses for a moment to measure the wind. It becomes his new habit.

Late in Bhadro, one noon, he is making a short flight over the stream. The sky is clear, but the movement of air along the hillside is restless. Crossing from one slope to another, a gust comes up from below and strikes him. His body spins, the balance of his wings is lost, and he falls into a narrow crack between two huge boulders. The crack is barely wider than his body. The walls are wet, slick with moss, and above is a strip of sky. He tries to open his wings, but the feathers scrape stone and bend. He beats once hard, his body rises a little, then drops again. The second time he beats harder. This time the edge of his wing strikes the rock and the pain spreads to his shoulder.

At first he is desperate to free himself. He opens his wings, folds them, opens them again. He scrapes the stone wall with his talons. But the crack is so narrow that his wings cannot fully open, and he cannot shift his weight properly. After a while he understands that if he keeps thrashing like this his strength will be gone. He stops. He lowers his head and breathes. Cold water stands on the stone. Clouds drift across the thin strip of sky above. On the first night fog comes down, cold, wet fog that creeps into the crack and soaks his feathers. He folds his wings against his chest and shivers all night. From the gaps in the rock below, water falls in drops now and then. He lifts his head and looks up. The narrow ribbon of sky is covered by cloud, then shows again. All his effort until now, the new feathers, the slow return of strength, will it all end inside this crack? He no longer beats his wings. He only waits.

In the morning he shifts and examines the wall of the crack. On one side there is a small ledge in the stone, on the other a root showing under the moss. First he takes the ledge with his good foot, then lifts the injured foot a little higher. His body rises an inch. He seizes the root in his beak and changes his grip. Another inch. Several times he slips and slides down. Sometimes he leans his body against the stone to rest, sometimes he hangs in one place for a long time. Before every climb he tests the place where his foot will go. At noon on the second day he reaches the middle of the crack. There is more light above, but the wall is more slick. When he steps onto a ledge, a small piece of stone breaks away. He drops several inches. This time he closes his eyes and holds still for a while. Then he catches a root on the other side in his beak, turns his body, and increases the grip of his talons. One inch, then another inch. As the light of the afternoon reaches the mouth of the crack, he gets to the rim. At that moment a current of warm air comes down over the hill. He opens his wings. He leaves the edge of the stone and lifts his body into the air. At first his wings tremble, then they take the weight of the wind and go still.

Back on his own slope the hawk sits a long time in the cleft. He has not eaten for nearly two days. There is dried blood near his beak, a few feathers at the edge of his wings are bent, and stone dust has settled on his talons. He makes no effort to clean them. He lets his body grow still. When evening comes he closes his eyes, and that night he sinks into a long sleep without dreams.

Ashwin comes. The rain thins, the gray of the monsoon lifts, and the slopes of the hills stand clear again. The wind is light, dry, warm, moving in layers. Most of the main feathers of his wings are new now, deep black, faintly glossy. The edges of a few are still not fully smooth, but the power to hold the wind has come back. He begins short flights, from one rock to another, brushing a slope and returning, sometimes going a little way over the stream and coming back toward his lair. After each flight he sits for a while. He wants to know whether something pulls inside his wing, whether his breath is running unnaturally fast. In two or three weeks small prey comes back to him too. One day a field mouse, one day a lizard from under a stone, one day a baby snake, which he eats whole, drawing it down carefully, little by little, from the head. His beak can tear hard food again. It is not as sharp as before, but there is strength enough to do the work. The grip of his claws is steadier than it was. After a kill he no longer has to sit a long time. Still he does not plunge blindly the way he once did. He measures the distance, studies the direction of the wind, and only then lowers his body.

His time in the air grows too, little by little, first a few moments, then a few minutes. One day he drifts a long way on the waves of the wind above the steep gorge of the stream. Below is a deep chasm, across it a green slope. The wind lifts him now, sets him down a little now. In midair a hollow in the wind makes his wing shudder, and his body leans to one side. At once he tilts his wing a touch and recovers the balance, then glides down to the slope below. He sits on a rock a long time, breathing. The next day he goes again. The wind has changed again, but he has read the direction beforehand. His wing does not shudder. He goes a little farther, then slowly circles and comes back to his own slope.

Around this time he sees the female a few more times. Sometimes she sits on a far ridge, sometimes she flies off with prey. One day the two of them rise at the same moment into the same layer of air. For a while they float side by side with a distance between them. The female turns her head once to look. The old hawk does not look at her, and does not drive her away. Their wings take the same wind, then one drifts toward the eastern slope and the other toward the south. Their paths part.

On a morning late in Ashwin the hawk goes to the top of the highest hillock and stands there. From the end of Boishakh to the end of Ashwin, a hundred and fifty-five days have gone by. Not one of them has been like another. Some days hunger, some days rain, some days the aching of his body, some days the failure of a hunt. Between them are the feathers that fell, the itching at the base of the new ones, the slow growth of the broken claw, the healing of the wound on his beak, the fear of the dive, and two long days trapped in a narrow crack of stone. Taken together, they have changed his body, but he has not got the old body back.

Kartik is only a few days away, and there is a faint chill in the air. The sun rises over the crest of the eastern hill, and its light falls on the sea, far off to the southwest, and glitters. On the ridge below, the female is drying her wings. She lifts her head once, then lowers it again. The old hawk does not stay looking at her. No urgency stirs in him, and no old emptiness either. She will live in her own sky. He will go his own way.

He spreads his wings. Once, the moment he opened them, the sky opened before him. Today, before opening them, he takes a moment to read the direction of the wind. The old pain in his shoulder is still there. The tip of his beak is not as sharp as it was. The broken claw on his right foot has not come all the way back. But he knows in what posture to hold his wings so that the wind will carry him, at what height the strain on his body is least, when to wait rather than dive. The limits of his own body are no longer strange to him.

He gives himself to the wind.

First he climbs straight up along the steep slope, then catches a warm current of air and goes higher. One great circle, then another. Below, the stony shelter shrinks until it is a single point. This time he does not have to come down to rest. The feathers at the ends of his wings hold steady without any struggle against the wind. He climbs higher, then turns southwest. Below him the green slopes of the hills, the cracks in the rock, the crowns of wild trees, all slowly drift away.

After a long while, in flight, he notices that the outermost feathers of his wings are bent again a little. The old habit has not gone. As though someone drifting beside him might brush against them, he has kept room. For a moment he turns his attention to those bent feathers. Then, slowly, he straightens them. The wind passes through the empty space, but this time it does not remind him of any lost body. It only passes beneath his wings and carries him forward.

Below, in the crack of the rock, a few faded feathers and one dry twig stay behind. He flies southwest, toward the sea, into a cloudless sky. The light of the sun on the sea grows brighter. Below, water, far off a shoal, and beyond it a coast he does not know. Where he will come down, when he will come down, whether he will come down at all, the decision is, for once, entirely his own. He goes on flying.
